title: ר' יהושע בן חנניה
author: Heilprin source tradition; Warsaw digital witness

paragraphs: (2) An unqualified ‘Rabbi Yehoshua’ in the Mishnah is ben Chananyah: Rashi, Nazir 56b. He was in Pekiin: Sanhedrin 32b. ‘Happy is she who bore him’ (Avot, chapter 2). Rashi explains that the Jerusalem Talmud, Yevamot, chapter 1, relates that when his mother was pregnant she would go to the twenty-four study houses in her town so that they would pray that the unborn child would be wise. [The checked commentary attributed to Rashi says all the study houses and gives no number.] That is the meaning of ‘Happy is she who bore him.’ But I saw in the Jerusalem Talmud, Yevamot 1:6, that Yonatan ben Harkinos applied to him ‘Whom shall he teach knowledge?’: ‘I remember that his mother used to bring his cradle to the study house so that his ears would cling to words of Torah.’ [In the checked Yerushalmi, the speaker appears to be Dosa, and the place is a synagogue.]

(3) He was a Levite. Rabban Gamliel gave him the tithe on account of his Torah learning, although Ezra had penalized the Levites; see Yevamot 86b. Rabbi Shimshon, in his commentary on the Mishnah at the end of Maaser Sheni, writes that he was given the first tithe because he earned his living with difficulty, as related in Horayot and Berakhot (see above), and the penalty did not apply to a poor person. Alternatively, according to Rabbi Akiva there in Yevamot, before the penalty it belonged specifically to a Levite, while after the penalty it could also go to a priest. He did not also give him the poor tithe, because one who gives all his gifts to one priest brings famine upon the world. Alternatively, he had two hundred zuz, but could still take the first tithe: Tosafot, Kiddushin 27a. He was a singer in the Temple, while his colleague Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudgeda was a gatekeeper: Arakhin 11b. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananyah wanted to help Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudgeda shut the doors. He told him: ‘Go back, my son, for you are among the singers and not among the gatekeepers.’ He said: ‘When we rejoiced at the water-drawing celebration, we saw no sleep’: Sukkah 53a.

(4) He was a student of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai (at the beginning of Demai, chapter 3, he went after Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai; Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai called Rabbi Yehoshua ‘the threefold cord,’ Avot de-Rabbi Natan, chapter 14). He was head of the court in the court of Rabban Gamliel, the Nasi of Yavneh; see his entry and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah. His colleague was Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus. In Niddah 7b, after Rabbi Eliezer’s death he upheld Rabbi Eliezer’s words. At the end of Gittin, 83a, he said concerning Rabbi Eliezer’s words: ‘One does not answer the lion after his death.’ Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer were among those young observers who expounded the letters mem-nun-tzadi-peh-kaf, which had been forgotten; see Rabbi Eliezer. At the end of Chagigah, 22b, he said: ‘I am ashamed of your words, House of Shammai.’ A student of the House of Shammai gave him a reason for their words. Rabbi Yehoshua immediately went and prostrated himself upon their graves, saying: ‘I have wronged you, bones of the House of Shammai.’ His teeth became black from fasting throughout his life. But the Tosefta, Oholot, end of chapter 5, has: ‘Rabbi Yehoshua did not go back to teach in accordance with the student’s words, and said, “I spoke to you, bones of the House of Shammai.”’ End quotation. Perhaps this is a scribal error and should read ‘Rabbi Yehoshua went back to teach,’ and ‘I have wronged you.’ He was greatly learned in the Chariot. While he was traveling with Rabbi Yose HaKohen, Rabbi Yehoshua began expounding the Account of the Chariot. That day was the summer solstice; the sky became covered with clouds, something like a rainbow appeared in the cloud, and the ministering angels gathered to listen, like people gathering to watch the merrymaking of a bridegroom and bride. Rabbi Yose HaKohen went and told Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, who said: ‘Happy are you, and happy are those who bore you; happy are my eyes that have seen thus.’ Chagigah 14b; see there. He was knowledgeable about sorcery and annulled the sorcery; his prayer caused Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira to be born—see there for an awesome story. [In the checked Yerushalmi the sages pray together.] Horayot 10a relates that he traveled with Rabban Gamliel on a ship. They lost their way at sea, and Rabban Gamliel’s food ran out, while Rabbi Yehoshua had food: he knew that a certain star rises every seventy years and leads sailors astray. [The checked text reports a delay and says Yehoshua brought provisions in case the star led them astray.] Rabban Gamliel wondered: ‘With all the wisdom you possess, have you no wealth?’ See Yuchasin, in the sequence of generations under Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudgeda. In Berakhot, the chapter Tefillat HaShachar, 27b: because Rabban Gamliel had troubled him—in Rosh Hashanah 25a and in Bekhorot—they removed the presidency from him and gave it to Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah; see his entry at length. Afterwards Rabbi Yehoshua was reconciled, and so forth. Rabban Gamliel said: ‘From the walls of your house it is evident that you are a charcoal worker.’ Rashi, Avodah Zarah 16b, explains that, because he occupied himself with Torah, he did not wash his clothing or body, as in Rashi’s explanation of ‘splendid wisdom in an ugly vessel.’ Rabbi Shimon Duran, in his Panim Chadashot, wrote that it is inconceivable that he, being head of the court, was a charcoal worker. Rabbenu Chananel explains that he made needles; so too in the Jerusalem Talmud, the chapter Tamid Nishchat. [It is not there, but in the chapter Tefillat HaShachar, at the end of its first mishnah, and in Taanit, chapter 4, at the end of halakhah 1:] ‘He found him making needles.’ Yet it says explicitly in the Jerusalem Talmud that he made charcoal. [This is not in the Jerusalem Talmud, but in the Rashi on Berakhot cited above.] Some say he was a smith [there in Rashi]. Sefer G.N. [ג״נ; provisionally Gilgulei Neshamot] writes that he was a reincarnation of Yehoshua the high priest—‘Is this not a brand rescued from fire?’—hence ‘You are a charcoal worker,’ and his face grew black. In the Mishnah at the end of Maaser Sheni, chapter 2, Rabbi Akiva said: ‘I converted R.N.’s [possibly Rabban Gamliel’s] and Rabbi Yehoshua’s second-tithe money into gold dinars.’ If so, Rabbi Yehoshua became wealthy. [The checked Mishnah names Rabban Gamliel. The inference about wealth is the compiler’s.] After R.N.’s [possibly Rabban Gamliel’s] death, Rabbi Yehoshua wanted to annul his words, but Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri did not allow him; see his entry. He went to learn Torah with Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri; see there. In Niddah 61a, there was a place containing ritual impurity which the sages could not examine. An elder named Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananyah was there. He brought sheets, soaked them in water, and spread them there: the pure place was dry, and the impure place wet. There, 25a, ‘Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chanina expounded’ should read ‘Chananyah.’ [The checked text already reads Chananya.] There, 69b, the twelve questions which the Alexandrians asked ‘Rabbi Yehoshua bar Chanina’ should read ‘Chananyah.’ In Eruvin, chapter 5, 53b, and tractate Derekh Eretz, chapter 6, a woman, a boy, and a girl bested him. In chapter 5 of the Laws of Derekh Eretz, R.N. [possibly Rabban Gamliel], Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, and Rabbi Akiva were traveling, and Rabbi Yehoshua said to R.N. [possibly Rabban Gamliel]: ‘Let us go greet our philosopher friend,’ and so forth. ‘Later generations: Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua, and Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai’ (Shir HaShirim Rabbah). He was present at the deaths of Rabban Gamliel the Elder and Rabbi Eliezer; see their entries. ‘When Rabbi Yehoshua died, goodness ceased from the world’ (Mishnah, the chapter Eglah Arufah). In the Tosefta at the end of Eruvin: ‘The laws of Shabbat, festival offerings, and sacrilege are like mountains hanging by a hair: little Scripture and many laws, and they have nothing upon which to rely. From this Rabbi Yehoshua said: Tongs are made with tongs; how did the first tongs come to be? Surely they were a created thing.’ End quotation. It appears that he lived long, since he survived Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer.

(5) When Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua disagree, the law follows Rabbi Yehoshua (Sefer Keritot; see Sheerit Yosef 38b). Halikhot Olam 33b writes that the law follows Rabbi Eliezer: this is a scribal error. [The checked Halikhot Olam records Eliezer and gives Yehoshua as Yosef Karo’s correction.] See Responsa Chavvot Yair, section 94.

(6) He was influential in the household of Emperor Trajan, as related in the chapter Ellu Terefot, 59b. The emperor said to him: ‘Your God is compared to a lion. What is the greatness in that?’ He replied: ‘He is compared to the lion of Bei Ilai.’ The emperor told him to show it to him. He prayed; when it was four hundred parasangs away it roared, and all the pregnant women miscarried and Rome’s walls fell. When it was three hundred parasangs away it roared, and his molars and teeth fell out, and the king fell from his throne. [The checked Chullin ascribes the loss of teeth to the people and leaves the emperor unnamed.] He begged him to pray for it to return to its place, and so it did. See there further for what he did to the emperor and the emperor’s daughter. In Berakhot 56a, beginning, the emperor told him to tell him what he would see in a dream, and so forth. In Shabbat 119a he asked why Sabbath food gives off its fragrance. In Bekhorot 8b he asked how long a snake’s gestation takes; he replied, ‘Seven years.’ He said: ‘But the elders of Athens say three years,’ and so forth. [In the checked Bekhorot the elders bred the snake and observed it give birth after three years.] He defeated those elders through several riddles, and so forth. It says there: ‘He hung suspended between heaven and earth’; see there at length. In Chagigah 5b a certain heretic gestured to him, and Rabbi Yehoshua responded by a gesture. The heretic did not understand, and the emperor had him killed. He went with Rabbi Eliezer and Rabban Gamliel to Rome to annul a decree (Devarim Rabbah, chapter 2). [The checked Midrash places the three in Rome when the decree was announced.] He traveled with Rabbi Eliezer, and Abba Yudan was there; see there, chapter 4. In Sanhedrin, Chelek, 90b, the Romans asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananyah: ‘Whence do we know that the Holy One, blessed be He, revives the dead and knows the future?’ In Taanit 7a and Nedarim 50b the emperor’s daughter told him: ‘Splendid Torah in an ugly vessel!’ [The checked Taanit reads “wisdom,” and Nedarim reads “Torah.”] He offered her the analogy of wine, which will not keep in silver vessels. In Bereshit Rabbah, section 64, and Yalkut, Toledot, the king decreed that the Temple be rebuilt, and Pappos and Lulianus supplied those returning from exile. The Samaritans denounced them, and the Jews wished to rebel against the government, and so forth; Rabbi Yehoshua consoled them—see there at length. Lulianus and Pappos were killed; see their entries. Shalshelet HaKabbalah 27b writes that this was about 290 years after the destruction. [The checked witness applies the date to the rebuilding effort.] That is an error, for he lived before the destruction and immediately after it. See Yuchasin, in the sequence of generations under Rabbi Akiva. Tzemach David, part 2, writes that this was in the year 3880. A certain king asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananyah: ‘Is it not written in your Torah, “For all His ways are justice”? How are His judgments righteous and His ways just, when we see Him harm one who has neither sin nor guilt? Some people are born with impairments—blind, lame, mute, or without an eye. Is that not injustice?’ Rabbi Yehoshua replied: ‘The good among them He afflicted to increase their reward in the world to come. As for the unbelievers among them, because of their evil conduct and their choosing the evil path rather than the good, He afflicted them before their creation. If you wish, my lord, I shall demonstrate this to you. Give me a thousand dinars and send with me two trustworthy men whom you trust.’ The king gave them to him, and they went with him until they encountered a man blind from his mother’s womb. Rabbi Yehoshua told him: ‘Know that the king has ordered my death. Let these thousand dinars remain deposited with you. If I escape him, return them to me; otherwise, let them be yours as a gift.’ The blind man took the money into his hand; the men witnessed this, and the blind man went on his way. After some time Rabbi Yehoshua came to the blind man and said: ‘Please give me the money I deposited with you, for the Holy One, blessed be He, has saved me and rescued me from the king. I shall pay you for your trouble and burden.’ The blind man replied: ‘By my life, I do not know you or anything you are saying to me, little or much. Nothing of the sort ever happened. You deposited nothing with me, and I am not a suitable person to hold a deposit.’ Rabbi Yehoshua told him: ‘If so, come with me to the king for judgment.’ They both went before the king. He said, ‘Give me my deposit,’ and the other said, ‘I know nothing of it.’ The king told him: ‘Bring evidence for your words.’ He brought the two trustworthy men, and they testified to the king that the blind man had received a thousand dinars from Rabbi Yehoshua. The blind man replied to the king: ‘My lord, this is not true; he never gave me anything.’ The king ordered him hanged. As they were taking him on the way to hang him, a certain man came and whispered in his ear: ‘I heard your wife talking and laughing with so-and-so, telling him: Wait until my blind husband dies, and I shall marry you, and we shall eat up the thousand dinars together.’ When the blind man heard this, he cried out loudly: ‘Untie me, and I shall go bring the dinars!’ They untied him, and he brought the dinars. Rabbi Yehoshua told him: ‘You did all this to me even though I gave the money before two righteous witnesses; how much more so had I given it without witnesses! But without doubt your Maker formed you blind in justice and truth.’ The king replied: ‘True and certain: your God is righteous in judgment and upright in His measures, and there is no injustice before Him’ (a small book of tales, Sefer Katan Maasiyot).

(7) Onkelos the convert received from him; see Aquilas. Rabbi Ilai, Rabbi Yehudah’s father, was before him. Rabbi Eliezer was his colleague. Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah is also listed. Rabbi Elazar ben Yehudah transmitted in his name. Rabbi Elazar Chisma (see above) and Rabbi Yochanan ben Berokah went to greet him in Pekiin, and he asked them whose Sabbath it was: Chagigah and Bamidbar Rabbah, chapter 14. Ben Bag Bag disputes with him. Beruryah lived in his time—this requires examination. Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh: see above. Rabbi Zekharyah ben HaKatzav transmitted in his name, as did Abba Chanan. Chananyah was his brother’s son. He transmitted in the name of Rabbi Yehudah ben Petiri. He testified with Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira, and Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira was born through his prayer. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira disputes with him. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hyrcanus; Rabbi Yehoshua bar Mammal learned from him. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was his teacher, as was Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri. Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudgeda: see above. Yonatan ben Harkinos, and Rabbi Yose HaKohen: see above. Rabbi Yose transmitted in his name. He transmitted in the name of Abba Yose Chalifkora of Tivon. Rabbi Yakim of Chadid lived in his time. Rabbi Yeshevav transmitted in his name. Rabbi Yishmael was his student. He redeemed Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha. And Rabbi Nechunyah ben Elnatan; Rabbi Nehorai transmitted in his name, as did Rabbi Simon and Rav Safra. Rabbi Akiva was his student. Rabbi Yehoshua went to him when Rabban Gamliel issued his order concerning the Day of Atonement according to Rabbi Yehoshua’s reckoning, and he came to Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinos: Rosh Hashanah 25a. [The checked passage says Akiva went to Yehoshua and Yehoshua subsequently went to Dosa.] He testified with Rabbi Pappias: Rosh Hashanah 6a. And Rabbi Tzadok; Shimon ben Azzai transmitted in his name. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said: ‘Rabbi Yehoshua testified.’ He greeted Rabbi Shimon ben Zoma. And Rabbi Taddai transmitted in his name.
